node.name: Electric charge and conservation
node.description: Describe electric charge and its redistribution without treating charge as consumed by a circuit.
node.details:
Electric charge is a property of matter that comes in two kinds, positive and negative: like charges repel and opposite charges attract. Protons carry +e and electrons carry −e, where the elementary charge e is exactly 1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so ordinary charge comes in whole-number multiples of e. The SI unit of charge is the coulomb (C).

Charge conservation says the net charge of an isolated system never changes; charge can only move from place to place. Rubbing a balloon on hair moves electrons from one to the other, leaving equal and opposite charges behind. The same idea corrects a common misconception about circuits: a battery does not use up charge. The same charge circulates around the loop, and what the battery supplies and the load converts is energy. This topic underpins electric fields, current, magnetism, and atomic structure.

node.name: Distinguish joint configuration, task coordinates, and reachable workspace
node.description: Joint coordinates describe the robot arrangement, while task coordinates describe the output specified for a job.
node.details:
Joint coordinates describe the robot arrangement, while task coordinates describe the output specified for a job. A position-only task imposes different requirements from a task that also specifies tool orientation.

Workspace describes the outputs a robot can reach under stated limits. Reaching a point does not establish that every orientation at that point is possible, and different joint configurations may produce the same requested output.

node.name: Logarithms
node.description: Interpret a logarithm as an exponent and apply product, quotient, and power rules.
node.details:
A logarithm answers the question: what exponent produces this number? The statement log_b(x) = y means the same as b^y = x, so log2(8) = 3 because 2³ = 8, and log10(0.01) = −2. Logarithms are the inverses of exponential functions, so the base b must be positive and not equal to 1, and the argument x must be positive. The most used bases are 10, the common logarithm, and e ≈ 2.718, the natural logarithm ln.

Three laws turn multiplication into addition: log_b(xy) = log_b(x) + log_b(y), log_b(x/y) = log_b(x) − log_b(y), and log_b(x^p) = p·log_b(x). A frequent error is splitting log(x + y), for which no such rule exists. The change-of-base formula log_b(x) = ln(x)/ln(b) lets a calculator handle any base; for example, log2(10) ≈ 3.32. Logarithmic scales compress enormous ranges, which is why power gain in decibels is 10·log10 of a power ratio.

node.name: Trigonometric identities
node.description: Transform trigonometric expressions using angle and Pythagorean identities.
node.details:
A trigonometric identity is an equation that holds for every angle where both sides are defined, unlike an ordinary equation that is true only for particular angles. The core set includes the Pythagorean identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, the quotient identity tan θ = sin θ / cos θ, and the sum formulas sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B and cos(A + B) = cos A cos B − sin A sin B.

Double-angle formulas follow by setting A = B: sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ and cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ = 1 − 2 sin²θ. As an example, (1 − cos²θ)/sin θ simplifies to sin θ, because the numerator equals sin²θ. To prove an identity, transform one side until it matches the other rather than treating it as an equation to solve. Identities are essential for calculus integrals, amplitude-phase form, and stress transformations.

node.name: Electric force and field
node.description: Relate forces on charges to an electric field and use simple charge models.
node.details:
Charges push and pull on each other at a distance. Coulomb's law gives the size of the force between two point charges: F = k|q₁q₂|/r², with k ≈ 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²; like charges repel and opposite charges attract. The electric field E describes that influence as a property of space: it is the force per unit positive test charge, so a charge q placed there feels F = qE. Its units are N/C, equivalent to V/m.

Field lines point away from positive charges and toward negative ones, and a point charge's field has magnitude E = k|q|/r². For 1.0 μC at 0.10 m, E ≈ (8.99 × 10⁹ × 10⁻⁶)/0.01 ≈ 9.0 × 10⁵ N/C. Fields from several charges add as vectors, so direction matters as much as size, and a negative charge feels a force opposite to the field. These ideas explain capacitors, capacitive touch sensing, and the electrostatic attraction of dust.

node.name: Electric potential and voltage
node.description: Interpret potential difference as energy transfer per unit charge.
node.details:
Electric potential is electric potential energy per unit charge, and a potential difference, or voltage, between two points tells how much energy each coulomb gains or loses moving between them. One volt is one joule per coulomb, and the energy change for a charge q is ΔU = qΔV. Only differences are physically meaningful, so a voltage always compares two points; ground is simply the point chosen as the zero reference.

A 9 V battery moving 2 C of charge through a circuit transfers 18 J. An electron accelerated through 1 V gains one electronvolt, about 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. The electric field points from higher to lower potential, and in a uniform field the potential difference across a distance d along the field is ΔV = Ed, so 12 V across plates 3 mm apart means a field of 4000 V/m. Positive charges tend to move toward lower potential, negative charges toward higher potential.

node.name: Trigonometric and exponential derivatives
node.description: Differentiate exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions, keeping angles in radians.
node.details:
Beyond polynomials, the core transcendental derivatives are d/dx e^x = e^x, d/dx a^x = a^x·ln a, d/dx ln x = 1/x, d/dx sin x = cos x, d/dx cos x = −sin x, and d/dx tan x = sec² x. Combined with the chain rule, they give results such as d/dt e^(−2t) = −2e^(−2t) and d/dt sin(5t) = 5cos(5t), the building blocks for describing decay and oscillation.

The trigonometric formulas hold only when angles are in radians. They rest on the limit sin(h)/h → 1 as h → 0, which is true in radians but not in degrees; if x is measured in degrees, the derivative of sin x is (π/180)cos x. In the same way, e^x is special because it is its own derivative, while other bases pick up the factor ln a. Keep calculator modes and formulas consistent. These derivatives are essential for second-order linear differential equations, whose solutions combine exponentials, sines, and cosines.

node.name: Derive the Cartesian position Jacobian of a planar two-link arm
node.description: Differentiate the two planar tip-position equations with respect to q1 and q2.
node.details:
Differentiate the two planar tip-position equations with respect to q1 and q2. Arrange the derivatives in a two-by-two matrix whose rows correspond to x and y and whose columns correspond to the joints.

Use radians for angular derivatives and preserve the row and column order. This is a position Jacobian; a spatial twist Jacobian or a pose-parameter derivative may have different rows and interpretations.
node.placementNote: This connects the forward position model to local velocity relationships.
node.proficiencyReference: I can derive the planar position Jacobian and state the meaning of its rows and columns.

node.name: Calculate instantaneous planar tip velocity from joint rates
node.description: Evaluate the position Jacobian at the current configuration and multiply it by the joint-rate vector.
node.details:
Evaluate the position Jacobian at the current configuration and multiply it by the joint-rate vector. The result is instantaneous tip velocity expressed in the same Cartesian frame used for the position equations.

Keep revolute rates in radians per second when using radian-based derivatives. The same rates can produce different velocities at different configurations; a single local Jacobian is not an exact finite-motion model over a large joint change.
node.placementNote: This uses the derived Jacobian as a local velocity map.
node.proficiencyReference: I can calculate tip velocity and explain why the current configuration matters.

node.name: Identify lost instantaneous motion directions at a planar arm singularity
node.description: For the two-link position task, the Jacobian determinant is L1*L2*sin(q2).
node.details:
For the two-link position task, the Jacobian determinant is L1*L2*sin(q2). With positive link lengths it vanishes when the links are straight or folded, and the velocity map loses rank.

Inspect the available velocity directions rather than saying the robot cannot move at all. At full extension, radial tip velocity is unavailable to first order; inward displacement can still develop through a finite joint motion.
node.placementNote: This interprets the velocity map where independent task directions are lost.
node.proficiencyReference: I can identify the planar singular configurations and explain the local motion restriction.
